title: Impact of combining human and analytics feedback on students’ engagement with, and performance in, reflective writing tasks
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adding analytics-based behavioural feedback to tutor-provided content feedback can improve students’ engagement with and performance in reflective writing. The authors argue that reflective writing is difficult because it requires self-regulated learning, and that traditional feedback often focuses only on content while overlooking behavioural engagement patterns such as when and how regularly students write. The study asks whether combined human-plus-analytics feedback changes writing engagement, whether effects differ by students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) competence, and how engagement patterns relate to grades.

The intervention used Google Docs trace data to generate personalised behavioural feedback about students’ writing engagement. Both cohorts received the same tutor feedback on reflective writing content at mid-term. The intervention cohort additionally received an email in week 6 containing a graph comparing their engagement with cohort patterns plus suggestions encouraging regular weekly reflection. Analytics were based on time-series analysis of Google Docs revision logs, especially edited strings per day and regularity of engagement. The control cohort received only human content feedback.

The study took place in a single postgraduate course over two consecutive years at University College London. Eighty-one postgraduate students participated: 40 in the earlier-year control cohort and 41 in the later-year intervention cohort. Students completed weekly individual reflections across a 10-week course, with nine weeks of reflective writing contributing 40% of the final grade. The design was quasi-experimental rather than randomized because the two year cohorts served as comparison groups.

The authors conclude that combined human and analytics feedback increased students’ writing engagement relative to content-only human feedback. After the intervention, the treatment cohort showed significantly higher average daily edited content than the control cohort and more regular weekly reflection patterns. Regularity of engagement, especially active weeks and active days, was positively associated with reflective writing grades. Effects appeared particularly beneficial for students with lower SRL competence in terms of maintaining or regularising engagement, though statistically significant within-group change in quantity was clearest for high-SRL students. The authors caution that the study is limited by its non-randomized design, small sample, single institutional context, and lack of evidence about long-term sustainability across other settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with a comparison cohort, clear intervention, longitudinal behavioral measures, and statistical testing, but it is not randomized and uses postgraduate higher-education samples rather than K-12. The authors explicitly note cohort-based design limitations and limited generalizability.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects on engagement are in the small-to-moderate range, including a posttest between-group effect size of r=.34, which meets the >=0.20 threshold for medium impact. However, impact is clearest for engagement and less directly quantified for writing performance.

interventions.use_case: Personalized behavioral analytics feedback for postgraduate reflective writing, generated from Google Docs revision logs and time-series analysis, emailed to students alongside tutor content feedback to encourage more regular writing engagement.

finding.finding_summary: In a semester-long quasi-experiment with 81 postgraduate students, the intervention cohort receiving combined human content feedback plus analytics-based behavioral feedback showed higher reflective writing performance than the human-feedback-only control according to the authors’ interpretation, with better regularity of weekly reflection linked to better performance grades. However, direct between-group writing-score effect sizes for performance were not reported; reported evidence mainly shows correlations between engagement regularity and reflective scores (e.g., TotalActiveWeek r=.448, p<.001; AvgStrCountPerDay r=.353, p=.001; TotalRevision r=.293, p=.008).
finding.measure: Reflective writing performance grades / reflective scores

finding.finding_summary: The combined feedback intervention increased students’ engagement with reflective writing relative to human-feedback-only control. Within the intervention cohort, AvgStrCountPerDay increased from Md=1041.56 (IQR=1193.24, n=35 active-day observations) before feedback to Md=1354.17 (IQR=1669.83, n=34) after feedback, Wilcoxon Z=-2.162, p=.031, r=.26; after the intervention, the intervention cohort also exceeded the control cohort (Md=1354.17 vs 564.35), Mann-Whitney U=369.00, p=.004, r=.34.
finding.measure: Behavioral engagement from Google Docs logs, especially average edited strings/characters per day and active writing days
finding.effect_size: r=.26 within intervention pre-post; r=.34 intervention vs control post

finding.finding_summary: The intervention particularly benefited students with lower self-regulated learning (SRL) competence by increasing the regularity of their writing behavior, although not all subgroup comparisons reached statistical significance on daily quantity measures. For the intervention cohort high-SRL subgroup, AvgStrCountPerDay rose significantly after feedback (Md=705.81 to 992.04; Z=-2.244, p=.025, r=.27), while descriptive evidence suggested low-SRL students increased weekly engagement frequency (editing twice or more per week from 22.86% to 35.71%).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning-related engagement regularity and persistence in reflective writing
finding.effect_size: r=.27 for intervention high-SRL subgroup; other subgroup effect sizes not_reported
